questions.question: How do you write a FizzBuzz program in Java?
questions.title: FizzBuzz Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **FizzBuzz**: print 1..n, but print **Fizz** for multiples of 3, **Buzz** for multiples of 5, and **FizzBuzz** for multiples of both (i.e. 15). The trap is **order**: check **15 (both) first**, then 3, then 5. Even cleaner is to **build a string** by appending 'Fizz' if divisible by 3 and 'Buzz' if by 5, printing the number only if the string is empty.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you handle the both-multiples case correctly and avoid redundant divisibility checks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking 3 and 5 before the combined 15 case, so 15 prints 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the string-append approach to avoid the ordering bug and keep it extensible

sections.title: FizzBuzz and Its Ordering Trap
sections.content:
**FizzBuzz** asks you to print numbers `1` to `n`, replacing multiples of **3** with `Fizz`, multiples of **5** with `Buzz`, and multiples of **both** with `FizzBuzz`. It's a warm-up that screens for the **ordering bug**.

If you check `% 3` first, the number 15 matches and prints `Fizz` - wrong. The fix in the if-else style is to **check the combined case (`% 15` or `% 3 && % 5`) first**, then 3, then 5, then the number. A cleaner, more **extensible** approach **builds a string**: append `Fizz` if divisible by 3 and `Buzz` if divisible by 5; if the string is still empty, print the number. This naturally handles 15 (both append) and scales to new rules without nesting.

sections.title: FizzBuzz (String-Build Approach)
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[i from 1 to n] --> B[out = empty]
    B --> C{i % 3 == 0?}
    C -- yes --> D[out += Fizz]
    C -- no --> E[skip]
    D --> F{i % 5 == 0?}
    E --> F
    F -- yes --> G[out += Buzz]
    F -- no --> H[skip]
    G --> I{out empty?}
    H --> I
    I -- yes --> J[print i]
    I -- no --> K[print out]
```

sections.title: Buggy order - 15 prints 'Fizz'
Correct - check both first, or build a string
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong order**: checking `% 3` before the combined case makes 15 print `Fizz`.
- **Redundant checks**: `% 3 && % 5` is the same as `% 15` - either is fine, just be consistent.
- **Off-by-one**: loop must be `1..n` inclusive.
- **Hard to extend**: nested if-else gets messy if rules grow (7 -> 'Bazz'); the string approach scales.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Multiples of **3 -> Fizz**, **5 -> Buzz**, **both (15) -> FizzBuzz**.
- Check the **combined case first** in if-else order.
- The **string-build** approach avoids the ordering trap and is extensible.
- Loop `1..n` inclusive; **O(n)** time.
- It's a screen for clean conditional logic, not algorithmic depth.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: FizzBuzz is a classic warm-up. I print the numbers from one to n, but for multiples of three I print Fizz, for multiples of five I print Buzz, and for multiples of both, which is multiples of fifteen, I print FizzBuzz. The thing it's really testing is whether I handle that both-multiples case correctly, because there's a subtle ordering trap. If I write the if-else with the modulo-three check first, then fifteen satisfies it and prints Fizz, and it never reaches the FizzBuzz case. So in the if-else style, I check the combined case first, either modulo fifteen equals zero or divisible by both three and five, then check three, then five, then fall back to printing the number. The approach I actually prefer, and would mention to stand out, is to build up a string. I start with an empty string, append Fizz if the number is divisible by three, append Buzz if it's divisible by five, and then at the end, if the string is still empty I print the number, otherwise I print the string. This naturally handles fifteen, because both appends fire and I get FizzBuzz, and there's no ordering to get wrong. It's also more extensible: if someone adds a new rule, like print Bazz for multiples of seven, I just add one more append line instead of rewriting a tangle of nested conditionals. It's O of n, and while it's simple, doing it cleanly signals I write tidy conditional logic.

questions.question: How do you check if a number is prime in Java?
questions.title: Prime Number Check Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **prime** has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. To test `n`, check divisibility only up to **sqrt(n)** - if no number in `2..sqrt(n)` divides `n`, it's prime. That's **O(sqrt(n))**, far better than checking up to `n`. Handle edge cases: numbers `< 2` are not prime. To find all primes up to n, use the **Sieve of Eratosthenes** in O(n log log n).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you optimize the loop to sqrt(n) and handle n < 2 correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looping all the way to n (O(n)) or to n/2, and mishandling 0, 1, and 2
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why sqrt(n) suffices (factors pair up) and mention the Sieve for ranges

sections.title: Checking if a Number Is Prime
sections.content:
A **prime number** is a natural number greater than 1 with exactly two divisors: **1 and itself**. The naive check tries every divisor from 2 to `n-1` - **O(n)**. The key optimization is to only check up to **sqrt(n)**.

Why `sqrt(n)`? Divisors come in **pairs**: if `d` divides `n`, so does `n/d`, and one of each pair is always `<= sqrt(n)`. So if no divisor exists at or below `sqrt(n)`, none exists above it either. That makes the test **O(sqrt(n))**. Edge cases matter: anything **< 2 is not prime** (0, 1, and negatives), and 2 is the only even prime. To find **all** primes up to `n`, the **Sieve of Eratosthenes** is the efficient choice at **O(n log log n)**.

sections.title: Primality Test Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[n] --> B{n < 2?}
    B -- yes --> X[not prime]
    B -- no --> C[i = 2]
    C --> D{i*i <= n?}
    D -- no --> P[prime]
    D -- yes --> E{n % i == 0?}
    E -- yes --> X
    E -- no --> F[i++]
    F --> D
```

sections.title: Primality in O(sqrt n) with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Looping to n or n/2**: only need up to **sqrt(n)** - factors pair up.
- **Mishandling < 2**: 0, 1, and negatives are **not** prime; return false early.
- **Overflow in `i*i`**: cast to `long` for large `n`.
- **`Math.sqrt` rounding**: prefer `i * i <= n` to avoid floating-point off-by-one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Prime = exactly **two divisors** (1 and itself), `> 1`.
- Check divisors only up to **sqrt(n)** -> **O(sqrt(n))**.
- Factors pair as `d` and `n/d`; one is `<= sqrt(n)`.
- Handle **n < 2** as not prime.
- For all primes up to n, use the **Sieve of Eratosthenes**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A prime number is a natural number greater than one that has exactly two divisors, one and itself. The naive way to test if n is prime is to try dividing it by every number from two up to n minus one, but that's O of n and wasteful. The important optimization is to only check divisors up to the square root of n. The reason that works is that divisors come in pairs: if some number d divides n, then n divided by d also divides n, and for any such pair, at least one of the two is less than or equal to the square root of n. So if I haven't found any divisor by the time I reach the square root, there can't be one above it either, which means n is prime. That brings the time down to O of square root of n. I also handle the edge cases up front: anything less than two, that's zero, one, and negative numbers, is not prime, so I return false immediately. In the loop, instead of computing Math dot sqrt, which can have floating-point rounding issues, I just continue while i times i is less than or equal to n, and I cast to long to avoid overflow for large values. If the question is instead to find all the primes up to some n, I wouldn't test each one individually; I'd use the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which marks multiples of each prime as composite and runs in about O of n log log n, much faster for a whole range.

questions.question: How do you find the second largest element in an array?
questions.title: Second Largest Element Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Track **two variables** - `largest` and `secondLargest` - in a **single O(n) pass**. For each element: if it beats `largest`, shift `largest` into `secondLargest` and update `largest`; else if it's between the two (and not equal to largest), update `secondLargest`. This avoids the O(n log n) sort. Watch the **duplicates** case (don't let the max's twin become 'second').

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you do it in one pass with two trackers instead of sorting, handling duplicates
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting (O(n log n)) when O(n) works, or returning a duplicate of the max as the second largest
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Initialize to Integer.MIN_VALUE and decide explicitly whether duplicates count as second

sections.title: Second Largest in One Pass
sections.content:
You can find the second largest by **sorting** (O(n log n)) and taking the second-from-last distinct value, but the better answer is a **single O(n) scan** tracking two variables: `largest` and `secondLargest`.

For each element `x`: if `x > largest`, the old largest becomes the new second (`secondLargest = largest`) and `largest = x`; else if `x > secondLargest` **and `x != largest`**, update `secondLargest`. Initialize both to a sentinel like `Integer.MIN_VALUE`. The subtlety is **duplicates of the maximum**: if the array is `[5, 5, 3]`, is the second largest `5` or `3`? Decide explicitly - the `x != largest` guard treats it as `3` (second **distinct** value).

sections.title: Two-Tracker Scan
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[largest = MIN
second = MIN] --> B{next x?} B -- no --> Z[return second] B -- yes --> C{x > largest?} C -- yes --> D[second = largest
largest = x] C -- no --> E{x > second AND
x != largest?} E -- yes --> F[second = x] E -- no --> G[skip] D --> B F --> B G --> B ```

sections.title: Sorting - works but O(n log n)
Single pass - O(n), two trackers
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting unnecessarily**: O(n log n) when a single O(n) pass works.
- **Duplicate of max as second**: without `x != largest`, `[5,5,3]` returns 5 - clarify the requirement.
- **Bad initialization**: starting at 0 breaks on all-negative arrays; use `Integer.MIN_VALUE`.
- **Arrays with < 2 distinct values**: handle the 'no valid second' case.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Track **largest** and **secondLargest** in **one O(n) pass**.
- On a new max, **shift** the old max into second.
- Guard `x != largest` to skip **duplicates of the max** (if second must be distinct).
- Initialize to **Integer.MIN_VALUE**.
- Beats the O(n log n) sort.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The simplest approach is to sort the array and take the second-to-last distinct value, but that's O of n log n, and I can do better with a single linear pass. I keep two variables, largest and second largest, both initialized to a very small sentinel like Integer dot MIN underscore VALUE so they work even with negative numbers. Then I scan the array once. For each element, if it's greater than my current largest, then the current largest becomes the new second largest, and the element becomes the new largest, I shift them down. Otherwise, if the element is smaller than the largest but greater than my current second largest, I update second largest. That gives me the answer in O of n time and O of one space, with no sorting. The subtlety I always raise is how to handle duplicates of the maximum. If the array is five, five, three, is the second largest five or three? It depends on whether we want the second largest value or the second largest distinct value. If we want it distinct, I add a guard so that I only update second largest when the element is strictly less than the largest, which makes the answer three in that example. I'd clarify that requirement with the interviewer. I'd also handle the degenerate case where the array doesn't actually have two distinct values, returning some agreed sentinel or throwing, rather than silently returning the sentinel minimum.

questions.question: How do you rotate an array by k positions in Java?
questions.title: Rotate Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Rotate right by k using the **reversal trick** in O(n) time, **O(1)** space: first **`k %= n`** (k can exceed n), then **reverse the whole array**, **reverse the first k**, and **reverse the rest**. The three reversals leave the array rotated right by k. The naive 'shift one position k times' is O(n*k); an extra-array copy is O(n) time but O(n) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the in-place reversal algorithm and the k %= n normalization
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting k %= n (k > n loops), or using O(n) extra space when O(1) is possible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Derive the three-reversal trick and handle k > n with the modulo up front

sections.title: Rotate an Array by k (Reversal Trick)
sections.content:
Rotating an array **right by k** moves each element k positions right, wrapping around. Two things to handle first: **`k %= n`** because rotating by `n` is a no-op and `k` may exceed `n`; and the choice of algorithm.

The elegant in-place method is the **three reversals**: (1) reverse the **entire** array, (2) reverse the **first k** elements, (3) reverse the **remaining n-k**. This is **O(n)** time and **O(1)** space. Intuition: reversing the whole array brings the last k elements to the front (but reversed), and the two sub-reversals fix their internal order. Alternatives: copying into a new array (O(n) space) or shifting one slot k times (O(n*k) - too slow).

sections.title: Three-Reversal Rotation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[k = k % n] --> B[reverse whole array]
    B --> C[reverse first k]
    C --> D[reverse last n-k]
    D --> Z[rotated right by k]
```

sections.title: Rotate by k with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `k %= n`**: when `k > n` (or `k == n`), indices break or you do useless work.
- **Wrong segment bounds**: first segment is `[0, k-1]`, second is `[k, n-1]`.
- **O(n) extra space**: the reversal method is O(1); don't copy unless asked.
- **O(n*k) shifting**: rotating one position at a time is far too slow for large k.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Normalize with **`k %= n`** first.
- **Three reversals**: whole, first k, last n-k -> rotate right by k.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.
- Beats the O(n) extra-array copy and O(n*k) shifting.
- For rotate **left** by k, rotate right by `n - k` (or reverse in the other order).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To rotate an array to the right by k, the slick in-place approach uses three reversals. But before anything, I normalize k by taking k modulo n, because rotating by the array's length is a no-op, and k might be larger than the array. Then the algorithm is: reverse the entire array, then reverse just the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n minus k elements. After those three steps, the array is rotated right by k, and it's done in O of n time and O of one space, completely in place. The intuition is that reversing the whole array brings the last k elements to the front, but they end up in reverse order, and reversing each of the two pieces afterward restores their correct internal order. Let me give a quick example. With one through five and k equals two, reversing the whole thing gives five, four, three, two, one. Reversing the first two gives four, five, three, two, one. Then reversing the last three gives four, five, one, two, three, which is exactly the original rotated right by two. The mistakes to avoid are forgetting the k modulo n step, which breaks when k is greater than or equal to n, and getting the segment boundaries wrong, the first segment is index zero to k minus one and the second is k to n minus one. There are other approaches, copying into a new array is O of n space, and shifting one position at a time k times is O of n times k, which is far too slow, so the reversal trick is the one I reach for. To rotate left by k instead, I just rotate right by n minus k.
